output.summary:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Menstrual Migraine with Aura — Preventive Treatment KEY FINDINGS:
1. MENSTRUAL MIGRAINE: Peak attacks 2 days before to 3 days after onset of menses; estrogen withdrawal is the trigger
2. MINI-PROPHYLAXIS: Frovatriptan 2.5 mg BID or naratriptan 1 mg BID starting 2 days before expected menses (6-day course); reduces attack frequency significantly
3. CONTINUOUS OCP: CONTRAINDICATED in migraine with aura (category 3-4 per WHO)
4. TOPIRAMATE: First-line preventive; reduces monthly attack frequency by ~50%; start 25 mg QHS, titrate to 50 mg BID over 4-6 weeks
5. PROPRANOLOL: Alternative first-line preventive 40-120 mg BID; effective; may affect exercise capacity
6. CGRP MONOCLONAL ANTIBODIES: Erenumab, fremanezumab — newer options for chronic migraine; effective for menstrual migraine CONCLUSION: Mini-prophylaxis with frovatriptan peri-menstrually plus sumatriptan for breakthrough attacks. Consider topiramate if monthly prophylaxis needed. Peri-menstrual mini-prophylaxis (frovatriptan) recommended; combined OCP contraindicated; topiramate or propranolol for monthly prevention

DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — SUMATRIPTAN PRESCRIPTION Findings: Sumatriptan 100 mg is appropriate. No current medications to interact. No contraindications. Take at headache onset, not during sensory aura. Can repeat once after 2 hours. CONCLUSION: Sumatriptan 100 mg (3 tablets per month initially) is safe and indicated. Sumatriptan 100 mg safe; no contraindications; take at headache onset

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura — no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential
EEG is not indicated for migraine with aura; reserve for cases where focal seizure is genuinely on the differential

differential.key_features: Seizure propagation is seconds, not minutes; no loss of awareness; no inter-ictal epileptiform discharges
Stereotyped 3-year recurrent pattern, young woman, no vascular risk factors — incompatible with TIA
Episodic stereotyped sensory marches are not the temporal pattern of MS attacks; no other neurological deficits
Hand-to-face march crosses dermatomes — central (cortical) origin, not peripheral

key_clinical_evidence: Hand-to-face sensory march over minutes is the hallmark of cortical spreading depression; the rate excludes seizure (seconds) and TIA (instantaneous)
Menstrually-related migraine is a recognised pattern and the criteria pack allows perimenstrual mini-prophylaxis
No imaging or laboratory test is required when ICHD-3 criteria are met and there are no SNOOP red flags

patient.history_present_illness:
A 32-year-old Hispanic woman was referred to the neurology clinic by her primary care physician for recurrent episodes of numbness and tingling that she has experienced monthly for approximately 3 years. Each episode begins with tingling in her left fingertips that slowly marches up the left arm to the left side of her face over 15-25 minutes. During this phase she may experience mild left facial heaviness. After the sensory symptoms resolve, she develops a severe right-sided throbbing headache (7-8/10) with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound that lasts 4-8 hours. She takes acetaminophen 1000 mg which provides only moderate relief. She has tried sumatriptan once (borrowed from a friend), which was very effective.

She has approximately 10-12 episodes per year, consistently occurring in the days before her menstrual period. She recalls her mother having similar episodes with 'numbness and headaches' that improved after menopause. She works as a school administrator and the episodes frequently interfere with work — she has had to leave early on multiple occasions. She is on no regular medications, has never smoked, drinks wine socially (2-3 glasses/week), and exercises regularly. She reports normal blood pressure at routine checks, no diabetes, no prior stroke or cardiac history, and no recent travel or infections.

On examination today (headache-free), the neurological examination is entirely normal with full strength, intact sensation, normal reflexes, and normal coordination.
